Devices in Class

Devices are the enemy of in-class engagement: distractions that cover our eyes, plug our ears, and dominate our field of vision. Devices are also absolutely central to learning and research: we use them to look up historical facts, organize notes, and navigate texts. What to do, what to do?

The “default” policy for this is that you are welcome to use your devices to take and reference notes unless otherwise specified. However, the instructor will frequently designate “no screens at all” exercises, and reserves the right to ask you individually to put away your devices.

Always

  • No recording of any kind (audio, video, photos of slides or classmates).
  • No headphones or earbuds in during class.

Sometimes: Screens-Down Time

From time to time, I will designate no screens or devices for part of a class session (for example, during discussions or handwritten evaluations). When that happens, put everything away until I say otherwise.

Laptops, Tablets, and Phones

Unless I say otherwise, you are welcome to use a laptop, tablet, or phone in class to:

  • Take and consult your notes
  • Consult the readings
  • Look up a name, date, place, or term that comes up in class
  • Take part in in-class polls, the live question forum, and other interactive exercises
  • Scan and upload handwritten work at the end of an assignment (see What to Bring in Course Format and Materials)

Devices are not for texting, social media, email, shopping, checking the latest scores, or work for other classes. The test is simple: is what’s on your screen part of this class session? Keep in mind that your screen is also in the field of vision of everyone sitting behind you.

If your device use becomes a distraction, I may ask you to put it away.

Fine Print

The no-recording rule follows the University of Pittsburgh’s recommended policy: students may not record classroom lectures, discussions, or activities without the instructor’s advance written permission, and any approved recording is for the student’s own private use only.

Accommodations through Disability Resources and Services (DRS), such as approved recording, assistive listening devices, or other assistive technology, take precedence over this page.
